Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "there is an outdoor chess table in the small public garden behind the library, and i have started thinking of it as a place that changes the pace of my errands. it is a square concrete table with a checkerboard set into the top, two metal stools bolted to the ground, and a narrow rim where people put their cups or keys. the black squares have gone a little gray at the edges. on the side nearest the path, someone has scratched a shallow line through one white square, but it does not stop the board from being usable. i pass it on my way to return books, and lately i have been stopping there even when i do not have a book to return.

at first i thought the table was mainly for people who already knew how to play. there is no sign explaining the rules, and the pieces are not supplied, so you have to bring them yourself. but the table seems to welcome people who are not in a hurry to prove anything. one morning, an older man set a small cloth bag beside his coffee and laid out a wooden set. the pieces were worn smooth, especially the knights, whose ears had been rubbed almost flat. he looked at the board for a while before moving, and i liked that he did not treat each pause as wasted time. i was sitting nearby with a paper cup, pretending to read a notice on the library door, though i was mostly watching the game.

when the man’s opponent arrived, she apologized for being late and said, “the bus came when it felt like it.” he answered, “then we’ll let the pawns wait too.” it was a small exchange, but it stayed with me because neither person seemed to be trying to make the other feel bad. they began without a handshake or a formal introduction. she took the white pieces, he took the black ones, and their first few moves were quiet. a child passing with a scooter asked why the pieces had different shapes. the woman explained that each one moved in its own way, and the child listened for a minute before going on. the explanation was plain and patient, not a lesson designed to show how much she knew.

1. what the table makes room for

i have noticed that the board is not only a surface for a game. it is also a reason to sit down next to someone without needing to invent an excuse. people arrive carrying grocery bags, library books, or a folded newspaper, and they set those things on the rim while they decide what to do. on a cool afternoon, two teenagers used the stools to sort out a disagreement about a school project. they did not play chess, but one of them moved a bottle cap across the squares while making a point. a few minutes later, they were laughing. i cannot say the table fixed anything between them; i only saw that it gave their conversation a place to continue.

there are marks of many kinds on the concrete. a pale ring from somebody’s drink sits near the corner, and a little cluster of initials has been cut into the underside where you would not see it unless you leaned down. after rain, water stays in one shallow dent and reflects a piece of the sycamore tree above it. the leaves sometimes drop onto the board, and people brush them away before they begin. once, a woman moved one leaf from a square and said, “there, now it can be a bishop again.” she smiled as she said it, but she did not turn the moment into a performance. i remember her line because it made the table feel less like public furniture and more like something people had learned how to share.

I am not a strong chess player. i know how the pieces move, and i can follow a game if nobody goes too fast, but i still overlook threats that seem obvious to the person across from me. when i tried a game with a neighbor, i kept glancing at the library clock and then apologizing for glancing. he said, “you can take your time; the clock is not playing.” i made a bad move a few minutes later, and he pointed out what i had missed without making a show of it. we did not finish the game because the library was closing and i had to return a book. i left with the sense that the unfinished position was not a failure. it was just where we had stopped.

the table has also changed the way i understand waiting. before, a pause between errands felt like time that needed filling: a message to answer, a list to check, another thing to get done. sitting at the board makes me look at the little choices people make. someone turns a stool so the sun is not in their eyes. someone else lays a scarf over the cold metal seat. two people may study the same position silently, each seeing a different next move. none of this is dramatic, and maybe that is why i can pay attention to it. i am not claiming that a chess table makes a neighborhood close or that every stranger becomes a friend. most days, people simply pass by.

still, i have begun to recognize a few regulars by the objects they bring: the wooden pieces in the cloth bag, the red travel set in a tin, the newspaper folded into quarters. i do not know all their names, and i do not know what they think of the table. sometimes there is no game at all, only the empty board with a couple of leaves on it. even then, the stools are turned toward each other, and the squares hold the light in a different way from the path. i usually sit for a few minutes before going on. it is a modest pause, but it has become part of how i move through this corner of the garden.", "output": "There is an outdoor chess table in the small public garden behind the library, and I have started thinking of it as a place that changes the pace of my errands. last saturday i spent most of the afternoon at the outdoor chess table in alder square, and i came away liking it more than i expected. the table sits near the path between the fountain and the small community garden, not right in the middle of the busiest part of the park. from the bench beside it, you can see people walking dogs and going toward the bus stop, but they don't have to pass close enough to interrupt a game. i had walked past it a few times before, usually when the board was wet, so this was my first proper chance to use it.

the concrete top is broad enough for two players to sit comfortably opposite each other, with a little room at either end for a bag or a drink. the board is set into the surface rather than painted on, and the squares are dark gray and pale stone. some of the dark squares have faded at the edges, though the pattern is still easy to follow. i measured the playing area later with my phone's measuring app and got about 20 inches across. that seems a sensible size for an outdoor board, not so small that the pieces feel crowded and not so large that you have to lean across the table for every move.

i brought my own pieces because the table doesn't have any attached or stored there. mine are a standard tournament set, and they worked fine, although the board's slightly rough finish made a few of the smaller pieces wobble if i set them down carelessly. the seats are also concrete, fixed in place, and a little lower than the chairs i use at home. after an hour i noticed the difference in my knees, but it wasn't painful. there is no back support, so this probably isn't where i'd choose to play a long match if comfort was the main concern. still, the surfaces felt sturdy, and nothing shifted when either of us leaned in.

i played two games with my neighbor, lena, who had brought a cloth bag of pieces. the first game lasted around 25 minutes. we started with no particular opening plan, and a couple of people paused nearby to watch. one man asked, “is this table open to anybody?” i said, “yes, as far as i know,” and he nodded before continuing along the path. that small exchange made the table feel public in a good way; it wasn't marked as belonging to a club, and we didn't feel we had to explain why we were using it. a laminated notice on the nearby garden fence gives the park's general hours, but it doesn't mention chess or table rules.

1) details that mattered during play

the table is under a large maple, which gave us shade for most of the afternoon. a patch of sunlight moved across one corner as the hour went on, but it never covered enough of the board to make the colors hard to distinguish. there were a few dry leaves in the grooves around the board, and i brushed them away before setting up. the surface wasn't perfectly level: a coin placed near the north edge slowly slid a little toward the center. it didn't affect our games, but someone who likes a completely flat board might notice it. the nearby path is paved and fairly smooth, although the route from the street includes one shallow curb that could be awkward for a wheelchair user without a curb cut nearby.

the setting was mostly calm, with the usual park sounds rather than silence. we heard children near the fountain, a delivery truck backing up on the next street, and a dog barking now and then. none of that made conversation difficult. there is a trash bin about a dozen steps away, and the garden fence gives the table some separation from the path without blocking the view. i couldn't find a water fountain right beside the table, so i was glad i'd brought a bottle. on a warmer day, that would matter more than it did for us; the weather was mild, and the shade kept the concrete from feeling hot.

lena said, “i like that it doesn't feel precious. you can just sit down and play.” i understood what she meant. the table has scuffs and a few small chips along the outer edge, but it doesn't look neglected. those marks made it seem like people actually use it, though i would still want the damaged corner checked before it became a sharp or larger break. i didn't see any loose parts, graffiti, or standing water, and the board was clean once the leaves were gone. there was no sign explaining whether the park staff clean the table on a schedule.

we switched colors for the second game and played more slowly. the fixed seats meant neither of us could adjust the distance from the board, but the space between them was comfortable for our height. when a cyclist stopped to look, i worried for a moment that we were blocking the way; then i realized the table is set back from the path far enough that people could pass on either side. we finished without feeling rushed. i didn't see another group waiting, but on a busy weekend the lack of a second chess table could mean players have to take turns.

overall, i found the table useful and pleasant for a casual game, especially if you bring your own pieces and don't expect indoor-chair comfort. i would choose it again on a dry day, and i'd probably bring a small cloth to clear the board before starting. the slightly uneven surface and fixed seats are real limitations, but neither stopped us from enjoying the afternoon. for me, the best part was having a simple place to play outdoors without needing to reserve anything or join a group.", "output": "Last Saturday, I spent most of the afternoon at the outdoor chess table in Alder Square, and I came away liking it more than I expected. The table sits near the path between the fountain and the small community garden, not right in the middle of the park’s busiest area. From the bench beside it, you can see people walking dogs and heading toward the bus stop, but they don’t have to pass close enough to interrupt a game. I had walked past it a few times before, usually when the board was wet, so this was my first proper chance to use it.

The concrete top is broad enough for two players to sit comfortably opposite each other, with a little room at either end for a bag or a drink. The board is set into the surface rather than painted on, and its squares are dark gray and pale stone. Some of the dark squares have faded at the edges, though the pattern is still easy to follow. I later measured the playing area with my phone’s measuring app and got about 20 inches across. That seems like a sensible size for an outdoor board: not so small that the pieces feel crowded, and not so large that you have to lean across the table for every move.

I brought my own pieces because the table doesn’t have any attached to it or stored nearby. Mine are a standard tournament set, and they worked fine, although the board’s slightly rough finish made a few of the smaller pieces wobble if I set them down carelessly. The seats are concrete, fixed in place, and a little lower than the chairs I use at home. After an hour, I noticed the difference in my knees, but it wasn’t painful. There’s no back support, so this probably isn’t where I’d choose to play a long match if comfort were my main concern. Still, the surfaces felt sturdy, and nothing shifted when either of us leaned in.

I played two games with my neighbor, Lena, who had brought a cloth bag of pieces. The first game lasted around 25 minutes. We started without any particular opening plan, and a couple of people paused nearby to watch. One man asked, “Is this table open to anybody?” I said, “Yes, as far as I know,” and he nodded before continuing along the path. That small exchange made the table feel public in a good way: it wasn’t marked as belonging to a club, and we didn’t feel we had to explain why we were using it. A laminated notice on the nearby garden fence lists the park’s general hours, but it doesn’t mention chess or table rules.

1) Details that mattered during play

The table is under a large maple, which gave us shade for most of the afternoon. A patch of sunlight moved across one corner as the hour went on, but it never covered enough of the board to make the colors hard to distinguish. There were a few dry leaves in the grooves around the board, and I brushed them away before setting up. The surface wasn’t perfectly level: a coin placed near the north edge slowly slid toward the center. It didn’t affect our games, but someone who likes a completely flat board might notice it. The nearby path is paved and fairly smooth, although the route from the street includes one shallow curb, which could be awkward for a wheelchair user because there isn’t a curb cut nearby.

The setting was mostly calm, with the usual park sounds rather than silence. We heard children near the fountain, a delivery truck backing up on the next street, and a dog barking now and then. None of that made conversation difficult. There’s a trash bin about a dozen steps away, and the garden fence gives the table some separation from the path without blocking the view. I couldn’t find a water fountain right beside the table, so I was glad I’d brought a bottle. That would matter more on a warmer day than it did for us; the weather was mild, and the shade kept the concrete from feeling hot.

Lena said, “I like that it doesn’t feel precious. You can just sit down and play.” I understood what she meant. The table has scuffs and a few small chips along the outer edge, but it doesn’t look neglected. Those marks made it seem like people actually use it, though I’d still want the damaged corner checked before it became sharp or developed into a larger break. I didn’t see any loose parts, graffiti, or standing water, and the board was clean once the leaves were gone. There was no sign explaining whether park staff clean the table on a schedule.

We switched colors for the second game and played more slowly. The fixed seats meant neither of us could adjust our distance from the board, but the space between them was comfortable for our height. When a cyclist stopped to look, I worried for a moment that we were blocking the way. Then I realized the table is set back from the path far enough for people to pass on either side. We finished without feeling rushed. I didn’t see another group waiting, but on a busy weekend, the lack of a second chess table could mean players have to take turns.

Overall, I found the table useful and pleasant for a casual game, especially if you bring your own pieces and don’t expect the comfort of indoor chairs. I’d choose it again on a dry day, and I’d probably bring a small cloth to clear the board before starting. The slightly uneven surface and fixed seats are real limitations, but neither stopped us from enjoying the afternoon. For me, the best part was having a simple place to play outdoors without needing to reserve anything or join a group."}]
